title: Temporal trends in intake category data for animal shelter and rescue organizations in Colorado from 2008 to 2018
authors: Hawes SM, Hupe TM, Gandenberger J, Morris KN
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective: To investigate trends in animal shelter and rescue organization intake for dogs and cats in Colorado from 2008 to 2018. Sample: 482 animal shelters and rescue organizations that reported annual intake data to the State of Colorado Department of Agriculture for 1,086,630 dogs and 702,333 cats. Procedures: Total intake, intake for each of 5 Pet Animal Care and Facilities Act (PACFA) categories (stray, owner surrender, intrastate transfer, interstate transfer, or other), and community-based intake (total intake after exclusion of transfers) of dogs and cats were assessed in total and for each organization type (shelter or rescue organization). The number taken in per year, number taken in/1,000 capita, and number in each intake category as a percentage of total intake were analyzed with linear regression models. Results: Trend lines indicated that total dog intake increased over the study period, but there was no change when these data were adjusted for the human population. Additionally, cat intake decreased over time according to both of these measures. For dogs, the stray percentage decreased while the interstate transfer percentage increased over time. Cat stray percentages also decreased while owner surrender percentages increased. Rescue organizations showed the largest increase in dog interstate transfers. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Monitoring intake category trends at the state level can help guide resource allocation and policy decisions for both shelters and rescue organizations.

mcqs.q: According to a 2022 study of Colorado animal shelter intake trends from 2008–2018, which of the following most accurately describes the pattern observed for dog intake when adjusted for human population?
o: Total dog intake increased significantly even after adjustment for human population
Total dog intake showed no significant change after adjustment for human population
Total dog intake decreased significantly after adjustment for human population
Total dog intake data were not sufficient to draw conclusions about population-adjusted trends
mcqs.e: While absolute dog intake numbers increased over the study period, once adjusted for the human population (per 1,000 capita) there was no significant change — indicating growth tracked human population, not a true increase in per-capita intake.

mcqs.q: In the same Colorado shelter study (2008–2018), which intake category trend was observed for dogs over time?
o: Stray percentage increased while interstate transfer percentage decreased
Owner surrender percentage increased while stray percentage decreased
Stray percentage decreased while interstate transfer percentage increased
Interstate transfer and stray percentages both increased over time
mcqs.e: For dogs, the stray percentage decreased while the interstate transfer percentage increased over the study period. This shift reflects changing shelter intake dynamics and the growing role of rescue organizations in transporting dogs across state lines.

mcqs.q: In the Colorado shelter intake study (2008–2018), what happened to cat intake over time?
o: Cat intake increased both in total numbers and per capita
Cat intake increased in total numbers but decreased per capita
Cat intake decreased according to both total numbers and per capita measures
Cat intake remained stable in total numbers but increased per capita
mcqs.e: Unlike dogs, cat intake decreased over the study period according to both total numbers and per capita measures. The study also found that cat stray percentages decreased while owner surrender percentages increased.

title: Retrospective review reveals few complications of ovarian pedicle tie in 15,927 cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy at a large HQHVSN clinic and training facility in the United States: 2017–2018
authors: Rigdon-Brestle K, Accornero VH, Amtower M, Slater MR
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective: To determine the rate of complications associated with the ovarian pedicle tie procedure in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy and to examine whether cat characteristics or surgeon experience level were associated with complications. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Animals: 15,927 cats that underwent ovariohysterectomy with the ovarian pedicle tie procedure at a large high-quality, high-volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) clinic and training facility in the US between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2018. Procedures: Data were extracted from electronic and paper medical records. Complications examined included pedicle drop or tear, pedicle hemorrhage, and pedicle-related death. Complications were coded by a veterinarian blinded to surgeon experience level. Results: Only 19 of 15,927 (0.12%) cats had pedicle-related hemorrhage, and in all instances, hemorrhage was corrected intraoperatively without serious complication or death. No pedicle-related deaths occurred. Cat reproductive status, body weight, age, and surgeon experience level were not significantly associated with pedicle-related complications. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: The ovarian pedicle tie is a safe technique for ovariohysterectomy in cats when performed in a HQHVSN setting, with a very low rate of pedicle-related hemorrhage. Surgeon experience level did not significantly affect complication rates, suggesting the technique is learnable across skill levels.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective study of 15,927 cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy with the ovarian pedicle tie technique at a large HQHVSN clinic, what was the rate of pedicle-related hemorrhage?
o: Approximately 1.2% of cats experienced pedicle-related hemorrhage
Approximately 0.12% of cats experienced pedicle-related hemorrhage
Approximately 5% of cats experienced pedicle-related hemorrhage
Pedicle-related hemorrhage occurred in less than 0.01% of cats
mcqs.e: Only 19 of 15,927 cats (0.12%) experienced pedicle-related hemorrhage. In all cases it was corrected intraoperatively with no deaths, demonstrating the overall safety of the technique in a high-volume setting.

mcqs.q: According to this HQHVSN retrospective study, which of the following factors was significantly associated with pedicle-related complications after OHE using the pedicle tie technique?
o: Surgeon experience level — less experienced surgeons had higher complication rates
Cat body weight — heavier cats had higher complication rates
Cat reproductive status — pregnant cats had higher complication rates
None of the above — no factors were significantly associated with complications
mcqs.e: Cat reproductive status, body weight, age, and surgeon experience level were all NOT significantly associated with pedicle-related complications. This finding supports the learnability and broad applicability of the pedicle tie technique.

title: Daily gabapentin improved behavior modification progress and decreased stress in shelter cats from hoarding environments in a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial
authors: Eagan BH, van Haaften K, Protopopova A
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the impact of daily gabapentin on behavior modification progression and signs of stress in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments. Design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Animals: 37 cats from hoarding environments (32 met inclusion criteria). Procedures: Healthy fearful cats were entered into either a gabapentin (10 mg/kg PO q12h) or placebo group upon intake. Both groups received daily behavior modification. Daily measures of cat stress score, latency to emerge from hiding, general in-shelter behavior, and urine suppression were collected. Cats were deemed to have graduated from the program when they met behavioral criteria for adoption or upon shelter departure. Results: Of 32 fearful cats, 28 (87.5%) graduated from the behavior modification program in a median of 11 days (range, 4 to 51 days). Animals receiving gabapentin showed greater behavioral improvement over time compared to those given a placebo, including faster progression through the behavior modification program and lower stress scores. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Daily gabapentin can improve behavior modification success and reduce stress in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments. This finding supports the use of gabapentin as an adjunct to behavior modification programs for difficult-to-adopt cats.

mcqs.q: In a randomized controlled trial of daily gabapentin (10 mg/kg PO q12h) in fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments, what was the primary finding?
o: Gabapentin had no effect on stress scores or behavior modification progression compared to placebo
Gabapentin caused significant sedation that impaired behavior modification progress
Cats receiving gabapentin showed greater behavioral improvement and faster behavior modification program completion than placebo cats
Gabapentin was only effective in cats weighing more than 4 kg
mcqs.e: Cats receiving daily gabapentin showed greater behavioral improvement over time, including faster progression through the behavior modification program and lower stress scores compared to placebo. Overall, 87.5% of cats graduated from the program.

mcqs.q: In the gabapentin shelter cat study, what dose and frequency of gabapentin was used?
o: 5 mg/kg PO once daily
10 mg/kg PO every 12 hours
20 mg/kg PO every 24 hours
10 mg/kg PO every 8 hours
mcqs.e: The study used 10 mg/kg orally every 12 hours (q12h). This is consistent with doses used clinically for anxiolysis and fear reduction in cats.

mcqs.q: What percentage of fearful shelter cats from hoarding environments graduated from the behavior modification program in the gabapentin trial?
o: Approximately 50%
Approximately 65%
Approximately 87.5%
mcqs.e: Of 32 cats meeting inclusion criteria, 28 (87.5%) graduated from the behavior modification program in a median of 11 days. This high success rate supported the overall protocol combining gabapentin with daily behavior modification.

title: Vasectomy and ovary-sparing spay in dogs: comparison of health and behavior outcomes with gonadectomized and sexually intact dogs
authors: Zink C, Delgado MM, Stella JL
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: Objective: To compare health and behavioral outcomes for dogs that underwent vasectomy or ovary-sparing spay (hysterectomy) with sexually intact dogs or dogs that had undergone traditional castration or ovariohysterectomy. Design: Cross-sectional, web-based survey study. Sample: 6,018 dog owners who responded to a web-based survey between November 3, 2021, and January 7, 2022, providing valid surveys for 6,018 dogs including 1,056 sexually intact, 1,672 castrated, and 58 vasectomized male dogs and 792 sexually intact, 2,281 spayed, and 159 ovary-sparing spayed female dogs. Procedures: Owners were asked questions about orthopedic and other health problems, cancer, and problematic behavior. Results: Longer exposure to gonadal hormones, regardless of reproductive status, was associated with reduced odds of general health problems and both problematic and nuisance behaviors. No significant differences in health outcomes were identified between dogs that had undergone vasectomy versus those that were castrated, or between ovary-sparing spay and traditional spay. However, gonadectomized dogs had higher odds of orthopedic problems compared to sexually intact dogs and those retaining gonads. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: This study, the first to compare outcomes across all five reproductive statuses, suggests gonadal hormone exposure — regardless of reproductive status — is protective for overall health and behavior. Individualized reproductive surgery decisions should consider the potential health implications of complete gonadectomy.

mcqs.q: A 2023 JAVMA cross-sectional survey study compared health and behavioral outcomes across five canine reproductive statuses (sexually intact, castrated, vasectomized, spayed, ovary-sparing spayed). What was the primary finding regarding gonadal hormone exposure?
o: Gonadectomy at any age was associated with significantly reduced cancer risk
Longer exposure to gonadal hormones, regardless of reproductive status, was associated with reduced odds of general health problems and problematic behaviors
Vasectomized dogs had significantly worse orthopedic outcomes than castrated dogs
Ovary-sparing spay was associated with higher rates of pyometra compared to traditional spay
mcqs.e: The study found that longer gonadal hormone exposure — regardless of whether the animal was intact, vasectomized, or ovary-sparing spayed — was protective for general health and behavior. Gonadectomized dogs showed higher odds of orthopedic problems.

mcqs.q: In the Zink et al. 2023 survey comparing reproductive status outcomes in dogs, which group had the highest odds of orthopedic problems?
o: Sexually intact dogs
Vasectomized male dogs
Ovary-sparing spayed female dogs
Gonadectomized dogs (castrated or ovariohysterectomy)
mcqs.e: Gonadectomized dogs (traditionally castrated males and traditionally spayed females) had higher odds of orthopedic problems compared to sexually intact dogs and those retaining gonadal tissue. This is consistent with prior research on the role of sex hormones in musculoskeletal development.

title: Natural history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in cats from rehoming centers: The CatScan II study
authors: Novo Matos J, Payne JR, Seo J, Luis Fuentes V
abstract: Background: The natural history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) in cats has been mainly studied in cats referred for suspected heart disease. Few data are available on factors associated with development of HCM in cats without clinical signs at baseline. Objectives: To characterize the natural history of HCM in cats from rehoming centers and identify echocardiographic variables associated with HCM development. Animals: One hundred seven cats from UK rehoming centers without a history of clinical signs of cardiac or systemic disease at the time of adoption. Methods: Prospective longitudinal study. After rehoming, cats were reexamined with serial echocardiography over a median follow-up of 5.6 years. Results: At baseline, 68 cats were echocardiographically normal, 18 were equivocal, and 21 had HCM. Nineteen additional cats developed HCM during follow-up. Lower left atrial fractional shortening, higher left ventricular fractional shortening, and higher body weight at baseline predicted HCM development. Cardiovascular events occurred in 21% of cats with HCM. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Lower left atrial systolic function appears to precede overt HCM in cats from rehoming centers. The prevalence of HCM in this unselected population was substantial, and cardiovascular events occurred in a meaningful proportion of affected cats, highlighting the importance of cardiac screening in shelter and rehoming populations.

mcqs.q: The CatScan II study (2022) prospectively followed cats from UK rehoming centers over a median of 5.6 years. Which echocardiographic variable at baseline was associated with subsequent HCM development?
o: Increased left atrial fractional shortening
Decreased left ventricular fractional shortening
Lower left atrial fractional shortening
Decreased body weight
mcqs.e: Lower left atrial fractional shortening (reduced LA systolic function) at baseline was predictive of HCM development. This finding suggests that subclinical left atrial dysfunction precedes overt HCM, making it a potential early screening marker.

mcqs.q: In the CatScan II study of cats from UK rehoming centers, what proportion of cats with HCM experienced cardiovascular events during follow-up?
o: Approximately 5%
Approximately 21%
Approximately 50%
Approximately 75%
mcqs.e: Cardiovascular events occurred in 21% of cats with HCM during the follow-up period. This meaningful event rate in an unselected rehoming population underscores the importance of cardiac screening in shelter and adoption settings.

mcqs.q: In the CatScan II study, what was the echocardiographic status of cats at baseline enrollment (from rehoming centers, no prior cardiac symptoms)?
o: All cats were echocardiographically normal at baseline
68 normal, 18 equivocal, 21 with HCM — showing significant pre-existing cardiac disease even in asymptomatic shelter cats
All cats had mild-to-moderate HCM at enrollment
Only stray cats showed pre-existing cardiac abnormalities; surrendered cats were normal
mcqs.e: Of 107 cats without prior cardiac symptoms, 21 already had HCM at baseline enrollment and 18 were equivocal. This demonstrates that significant cardiac disease is present even in asymptomatic cats from rehoming populations.

title: Renal amyloid-A amyloidosis in cats: Characterization of proteinuria and biomarker discovery, and associations with kidney histology
authors: Palizzotto C, Ferri F, Callegari C, Rossi F, Manfredi M, Carcangiu L, Gerardi G, Ferro S, Cavicchioli L, Müller E, Weiss M, Vogt AC, Lavatelli F, Ricagno S, Hurley K, Zini E
abstract: Background: Systemic AA amyloidosis recently was shown to have a high prevalence in shelter cats in Italy and was associated with azotemia and proteinuria. Objectives: To investigate urine protein profiles and identify diagnostic biomarkers in cats with renal AA amyloidosis. Animals: Twenty-nine shelter cats. Methods: Case-control study. Cats with renal proteinuria that died or were euthanized between 2018 and 2021 were included. Histology was used to characterize renal damage; immunohistochemistry confirmed AA amyloidosis. Urine protein-to-creatinine (UPC) and urine amyloid A-to-creatinine (UAAC) ratios were calculated. Urine protein profiling was done using sodium dodecyl sulfate-agarose gel electrophoresis (SDS-AGE) and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Results: Nineteen cats had AA amyloidosis. Affected cats had higher UPC and UAAC ratios than unaffected cats. Mixed proteinuria was identified in 89.4% of affected cats. LC-MS identified 63 potential biomarkers; urine apolipoprotein C-III was higher in cats with AA amyloidosis. AA amyloidosis was associated with glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats is associated with mixed proteinuria, specific kidney lesions, and elevated urine biomarkers. Urine apolipoprotein C-III may assist in diagnosis. Further research is needed regarding the role of lipid transport proteins in this condition.

mcqs.q: A 2024 JVIM study investigated renal AA amyloidosis in shelter cats in Italy. What type of proteinuria was most common in affected cats?
o: Purely glomerular proteinuria
Purely tubular proteinuria
Mixed proteinuria (identified in 89.4% of affected cats)
No proteinuria — only azotemia was present
mcqs.e: Mixed proteinuria (both glomerular and tubular components) was identified in 89.4% of affected shelter cats. This pattern reflects the combined glomerular and interstitial/tubular kidney damage seen in AA amyloidosis.

mcqs.q: In the shelter cat AA amyloidosis study (Palizzotto et al. 2024), which urinary biomarker was significantly elevated in affected cats on LC-MS analysis?
o: Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio only
Urine apolipoprotein C-III
Urine creatinine kinase
Urinary immunoglobulin light chains
mcqs.e: LC-MS identified 63 potential biomarkers, with urine apolipoprotein C-III notably higher in cats with AA amyloidosis. This finding points toward a role for lipid transport proteins in the disease process.

mcqs.q: What histologic lesions were associated with renal AA amyloidosis in the Italian shelter cat study (Palizzotto et al. 2024)?
o: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and tubular necrosis
Glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis
Mesangial proliferation and papillary necrosis
Diffuse amyloid deposition only in tubular lumens
mcqs.e: AA amyloidosis in shelter cats was associated with glomerulosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis on histology. These findings explain the mixed (glomerular and tubular) proteinuria pattern observed in affected cats.

title: Feline panleukopenia virus DNA shedding following modified live virus vaccination in a shelter setting
authors: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Ha K, Giacinti JA, Weese JS
abstract: This study assessed the frequency and timing of feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) DNA shedding in feces following administration of a modified live FPV vaccine in a shelter setting. Feces were collected from 37 shelter cats that did not meet clinical criteria for panleukopenia on the day of vaccination (day 0) or on days 3, 7, 14, and 21 post-vaccination. A commercial quantitative PCR (qPCR) fecal pathogen panel and a canine parvovirus point-of-care antigen test were performed on each sample. Positive qPCR results were obtained from 8/37 cats (21.6%) without clinical signs, primarily on day 7. DNA copy numbers were substantially lower following vaccination than in clinically infected cats. The point-of-care antigen test was negative in all vaccinated cats. FPV qPCR cannot differentiate subclinical infection from vaccine virus shedding. The authors recommend limiting PCR testing to cats with strong clinical suspicion of panleukopenia and considering recent vaccination timing when interpreting results, to avoid unnecessary outbreak responses based on false-positive PCR results in vaccinated shelter cats.

mcqs.q: A study of feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) DNA shedding in vaccinated shelter cats (Jacobson et al. 2022) found that positive qPCR results were obtained in what proportion of clinically healthy vaccinated cats?
o: Less than 1% of vaccinated cats
Approximately 5% of vaccinated cats
Approximately 21.6% of vaccinated cats
Greater than 50% of vaccinated cats
mcqs.e: 21.6% of vaccinated shelter cats (8/37) tested positive on fecal qPCR, primarily on day 7 post-vaccination. This is crucial for shelter medicine: positive PCR does not confirm active panleukopenia in recently vaccinated cats.

mcqs.q: In shelter cats vaccinated with modified live FPV vaccine, which diagnostic test remained negative despite qPCR positivity in some cats?
o: ELISA for FPV antibodies
Fecal immunofluorescence assay
Point-of-care antigen test
Virus neutralization assay
mcqs.e: The point-of-care antigen test was negative in all vaccinated cats, even those with positive qPCR. This suggests antigen tests may be more specific than PCR for distinguishing vaccine shedding from true infection in a shelter setting.

mcqs.q: Based on the FPV vaccine shedding study, what is the most clinically important implication for shelter medicine practice?
o: Modified live FPV vaccines should not be used in shelters due to shedding risk
All PCR-positive shelter cats should be immediately isolated for 21 days regardless of clinical signs
FPV qPCR results should be interpreted in the context of recent vaccination status; PCR should be reserved for cats with clinical signs of panleukopenia
Antigen testing should replace vaccination in shelter populations
mcqs.e: The study's main clinical message is that FPV qPCR cannot differentiate vaccine shedding from subclinical infection, so PCR should be limited to cats with clinical suspicion and recent vaccination timing must be considered — avoiding unnecessary outbreak responses.

title: Identification of spayed and neutered cats and dogs: Veterinary training and compliance with practice guidelines
authors: Mielo MR, Amirian ES, Levy JK
abstract: Spay/neuter identification tattoos and ear-tipping are simple, cost-effective methods to minimize unnecessary anesthesia and surgery in companion animals, or the misidentification of sexually intact animals. This study assessed training of sterilization identifiers in US and Canadian veterinary schools and practitioner compliance with guidelines for identifiers via surveys conducted in 2019. Faculty in all 34 participating veterinary schools reported curricula included sterilization identifiers in 31% of lecture-based training, 75% of spay/neuter laboratory-based training, and 38% of clinical practice-based training. A total of 425 facilities performing spay/neuter reported frequency and technical aspects of sterilization identifiers. Facilities encountering large numbers of animals of unknown background, performing a high number of surgeries, or with specialized spay/neuter training were significantly more likely to use identifiers. Only 5% of private practices tattooed all owned animals and 21% tattooed all unowned animals. In contrast, 80% of shelters and 72% of spay/neuter clinics tattooed animals. Green tattoos placed near surgical incisions represented the predominant technique. Enhanced training and broader implementation of sterilization identification best practices are essential to prevent unnecessary surgeries and unintended breeding in animals misidentified as sexually intact.

mcqs.q: A 2022 Veterinary Journal survey study found that what percentage of private veterinary practices tattooed all owned animals as sterilization identifiers?
o: Approximately 80%
Approximately 50%
Approximately 21%
Approximately 5%
mcqs.e: Only 5% of private practices tattooed all owned animals, compared to 80% of shelters and 72% of spay/neuter clinics. This gap highlights poor uptake of sterilization identification practices in private practice settings.

mcqs.q: In the sterilization identifier survey (Mielo et al. 2022), what was the predominant tattooing technique used to identify spayed/neutered animals?
o: Blue tattoo on the inner pinna
Green tattoo placed near the surgical incision
Black tattoo on the medial thigh
Ear notch combined with a microchip notation
mcqs.e: Green tattoos placed near the surgical incision site were the predominant identification technique. This is consistent with professional guidelines recommending a visible green linear tattoo at or near the incision for OHE/castration marking.

mcqs.q: According to Mielo et al. 2022, which types of facilities were significantly more likely to use sterilization identifiers?
o: Private practices with high small-animal case volume
Facilities with large numbers of animals of unknown background, high surgical volume, or specialized spay/neuter training
University teaching hospitals exclusively
Rural mixed-practice facilities
mcqs.e: Facilities handling large numbers of animals of unknown sterilization background, performing high numbers of surgeries, or with specialized spay/neuter training were significantly more likely to use sterilization identifiers — explaining why shelters and HQHVSN clinics have the highest compliance rates.

title: Capturing free-roaming dogs for sterilisation: A multi-site study in Goa, India
authors: Fielding HR, Fernandes KA, Amulya VR, Belgayer D, Misquita A, Kenny R, Gibson AD, Gamble L, Bronsvoort BMdC, Mellanby RJ, Mazeri S
abstract: Street and free-roaming dog populations in low- and middle-income countries pose public health risks including rabies transmission. Surgical sterilisation campaigns are a key component of humane dog population management. This multi-site study documented dog capture rates across six sterilization campaigns in Goa, India, using spatial coordinates and population surveys to assess campaign efficiency. Results demonstrate that as sterilization coverage increases within a community, capturing remaining intact dogs becomes progressively more difficult, with corresponding escalation in unit costs per dog captured. The study quantified diminishing returns on capture efficiency as the proportion of sterilized animals rises. These findings have important implications for planning efficient, cost-effective dog population management interventions: targeting areas of lower coverage first and adapting capture strategies as coverage improves may maximize program impact. Understanding capture dynamics is essential for sustainable free-roaming dog population control programs.

mcqs.q: A multi-site study in Goa, India (Fielding et al. 2023) examined dog capture efficiency across six surgical sterilisation campaigns. What key operational finding was identified?
o: Capture rates improved progressively as sterilization coverage increased due to community trust
Capture rates remained constant regardless of sterilization coverage in the area
As sterilization coverage increased, capturing remaining intact dogs became progressively more difficult with rising unit costs
Urban areas showed higher capture rates than rural areas across all campaigns
mcqs.e: The study found diminishing returns in capture efficiency: as sterilization coverage rises, remaining intact dogs become harder to capture and unit costs per dog increase. This has critical implications for planning sustainable free-roaming dog population management programs.

mcqs.q: Based on the Goa free-roaming dog capture study, what is the most important practical implication for designing humane dog population management programs?
o: Programs should cease operations once 50% coverage is achieved as additional gains are not cost-effective
Targeting areas of lower sterilization coverage first and adapting strategies as coverage improves may maximize program efficiency
Urban campaigns should be prioritized over rural campaigns in all low-income settings
Only government-run programs can achieve sufficient sterilization coverage for population impact
mcqs.e: The study's primary implication is to target areas with lower existing coverage first, and adapt capture methods as coverage increases — accounting for the progressive difficulty and rising costs of capturing remaining intact dogs in well-covered areas.

title: Frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs and cats: Results of a retrospective serological survey in Šumadija District, Serbia
authors: Stanojevic S, Radojicic S, Misic D, Srejic D, Vasiljevic DV, Prokic K, Ilic N
abstract: This retrospective serosurvey examined SARS-CoV-2 exposure in companion and stray animals in Šumadija District, Serbia, during the COVID-19 pandemic. A total of samples from dogs and cats were tested using a neutralization assay. The relative frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection in dogs was 1.45% and in cats was 5.56%. Pet owner seropositivity was 11%, and seropositivity in pets with close owner contact was 9%. Stray animals showed lower seroprevalence compared to household pets. The results confirm that companion dogs and cats are susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, with cats showing higher seroprevalence than dogs. Human-to-pet transmission was identified as the primary infection route. Findings emphasize the importance of One Health surveillance including companion and stray animals during respiratory virus pandemics.

mcqs.q: A Serbian serosurvey (Stanojevic et al. 2022) compared SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence in dogs versus cats. Which species had higher seroprevalence, and what was the approximate frequency?
o: Dogs had higher seroprevalence at approximately 5.56%
Cats had higher seroprevalence at approximately 5.56%; dogs at 1.45%
Dogs and cats had equal seroprevalence at approximately 3%
Neither species showed measurable seroprevalence
mcqs.e: Cats had higher SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence (5.56%) compared to dogs (1.45%), consistent with other studies showing greater susceptibility of cats to SARS-CoV-2. This is relevant to shelter medicine biosecurity during respiratory virus pandemics.

mcqs.q: In the Serbian SARS-CoV-2 serosurvey of companion and stray animals, what was identified as the primary route of animal infection?
o: Animal-to-animal transmission, particularly in multi-pet households
Human-to-pet transmission
Environmental contamination (fomite) transmission
Pet-to-human reverse zoonotic transmission
mcqs.e: Human-to-pet transmission was identified as the primary route of SARS-CoV-2 infection in companion animals. Pet owner seropositivity (11%) correlated with pet seropositivity (9% in close-contact pets), supporting this directionality.

mcqs.q: The Serbian SARS-CoV-2 serosurvey found that stray animals had lower seroprevalence compared to household pets. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
o: Stray animals have stronger innate immunity than companion animals
Stray animals had less close, prolonged contact with SARS-CoV-2-positive humans compared to household pets
Stray animals were vaccinated against COVID-19 in the survey region
The sampling methodology underrepresented stray cats which are more susceptible
mcqs.e: Stray animals had lower seroprevalence because they have less frequent and less prolonged close contact with humans, reducing their exposure to SARS-CoV-2 from infected owners. This supports human-to-pet as the dominant transmission route.

title: Top-down animal welfare crisis communication during the COVID-19 pandemic: Animal care worker information sources, self-perceived knowledge and welfare concerns
authors: Miller SL, Kwan JX, Dalton KR, Waite KB, Davis MF
abstract: This cross-sectional study assessed animal care worker responses to identify factors valuable for crisis preparedness planning during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants included small animal veterinary workers (n = 1,209) and shelter/rescue workers (n = 132). Shelter and rescue workers (SRC workers) more often reported frequent communication from their organization, self-perceived expert knowledge, and having welfare concerns related to the pandemic compared to veterinary workers. Information sources differed significantly by worker type, with SRC workers relying more heavily on organizational communications. The study highlights a potential need for increased, more harmonized crisis communication from leading public and animal health entities to better support both veterinary and shelter worker populations. Differences in crisis communication patterns between private practice and shelter workers may affect their ability to implement appropriate biosecurity and animal welfare measures during future public health emergencies.

mcqs.q: A 2025 Veterinary Record cross-sectional study compared small animal veterinary workers and shelter/rescue workers (SRC workers) during the COVID-19 pandemic. Which group more often reported self-perceived expert knowledge and animal welfare concerns?
o: Small animal veterinary workers
Shelter and rescue workers (SRC workers)
Both groups equally
Neither group — both reported low perceived knowledge
mcqs.e: SRC (shelter/rescue) workers more often reported frequent organizational communication, self-perceived expert knowledge, and having animal welfare concerns compared to private small animal veterinary workers. This suggests shelter workers may have heightened awareness of welfare implications during crises.

mcqs.q: Based on the Miller et al. 2025 crisis communication study, what was the primary recommendation for improving animal welfare crisis management?
o: Mandatory training for shelter workers in biosecurity protocols
Increased and more harmonized crisis communication from leading public and animal health entities to support both veterinary and shelter worker populations
Shelter workers should rely exclusively on CDC guidelines during pandemics
Private practices should be excluded from national animal welfare emergency planning
mcqs.e: The study recommended increased, more harmonized crisis communication from leading entities (e.g., veterinary associations, public health agencies) to address gaps and differences in information access between shelter and private practice workers — improving pandemic preparedness for the animal care workforce.

title: How do accessible veterinary care providers evaluate programmes and engage communities? Results of a qualitative analysis of Canadian service providers
authors: Rausch Q, Geddes N, Liao TP, Van Patter L
abstract: Accessible veterinary care (AVC) programmes aim to reduce barriers to veterinary services for under-resourced pet owners and communities. This qualitative study examined 18 Canadian accessible veterinary care providers through focus groups and interviews to understand how they evaluate their programmes and engage with communities. Analysis revealed large diversity in programme initiation, evolution, and evaluation approaches. Concerns identified included ethical challenges around community engagement, funder reporting requirements creating administrative burden, and limited knowledge and resources for rigorous programme evaluation. Providers highlighted the need for standardized metrics and evaluation frameworks to demonstrate programme impact. The study underscores the importance of community-centred, culturally appropriate service delivery and the need for better infrastructure to support AVC provider capacity for evaluation and long-term programme sustainability.

mcqs.q: A 2026 Veterinary Record qualitative study of 18 Canadian accessible veterinary care (AVC) providers identified which of the following as a key barrier to programme evaluation?
o: Insufficient veterinary staff to perform programme work
Ethical community engagement challenges, funder reporting burdens, and limited resources for rigorous evaluation
Lack of demand for accessible veterinary services in urban settings
Government regulations preventing low-cost veterinary service provision
mcqs.e: The study identified ethical community engagement challenges, funder reporting requirements creating administrative burden, and limited knowledge/resources for rigorous programme evaluation as key barriers facing Canadian AVC providers.

mcqs.q: What primary recommendation emerged from Rausch et al. 2026 regarding accessible veterinary care programme improvement?
o: AVC providers should prioritize high-volume spay/neuter over preventive care

mcqs.e: The study recommended standardized metrics and evaluation frameworks to help AVC providers demonstrate impact to funders and improve long-term sustainability — addressing the current lack of consistent evaluation infrastructure across these community-centred programmes.
